nameStory: Red deadnettle gets its curious name from its superficial resemblance to stinging nettle, but it's completely harmless — hence "dead" nettle. The "red" part refers to the reddish-purple tinge of its upper leaves and stems, which becomes more pronounced in cooler weather.
description: Red deadnettle is a low-growing annual herb that typically reaches 6-12 inches tall. It has a square stem (characteristic of the mint family) and heart-shaped, toothed leaves that are arranged in pairs opposite each other. The plant produces small, hooded purple-pink flowers clustered at the stem tips, and the upper leaves often take on a reddish-purple hue that gives the plant its name.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with scalloped edges, arranged in opposite pairs. Upper leaves often have a reddish-purple tint, especially in cool weather. Feel soft and slightly fuzzy, not stinging like true nettles.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, tubular purple-pink flowers with a hooded upper lip, clustered in whorls around the stem at leaf joints. Each flower is about 1/2 inch long and has a sweet, mild fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that forms small patches. Stems are square when rolled between your fingers and often have a reddish tinge, especially toward the top of the plant.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, brown nutlets in groups of four at the base of each flower cluster. Seeds are tiny and triangular, often dispersed by sticking to shoes and clothing.

habitat: Common in disturbed soils, gardens, lawns, roadsides, and waste areas throughout New England. Thrives in rich, moist soil but tolerates poor conditions. Often found growing alongside other weedy species like chickweed and dandelions in urban and suburban settings.

seasonality.spring: Emerges early and begins blooming in March-April. Young plants are bright green with less purple coloration in the upper leaves.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering through summer months. Upper leaves develop more pronounced reddish-purple coloring in response to heat stress.
seasonality.fall: Peak flowering often occurs in fall with cooler temperatures. Plants become more colorful as purple tinting intensifies in leaves and stems.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back, but seeds germinate in mild periods. In protected spots, small rosettes may persist through milder winters.

funFact: Red deadnettle flowers are edible and taste mildly sweet, making them a popular addition to wild salads. The plant can actually bloom year-round in mild climates, producing flowers even under snow cover during winter thaws.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with henbit deadnettle, but red deadnettle has stalked leaves (henbit's upper leaves clasp the stem directly) and more triangular leaf shapes. Remember: red deadnettle leaves have little "necks" or stems, henbit leaves hug the main stem like they're giving it a hug.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, red deadnettle is completely unrelated to stinging nettle and won't cause any skin irritation. The "dead" in deadnettle simply means "harmless" - early botanists used this naming convention to distinguish safe plants from their dangerous look-alikes.
compareHints: Red deadnettle differs from other Lamium species by its stalked, triangular-heart-shaped leaves and consistent purple-pink flower color. Henbit has stalkless upper leaves that clasp the stem, while white deadnettle is much larger with pure white flowers. Yellow archangel has yellow flowers and more deeply serrated leaves with silver markings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the deadnettles, henbit is unique for its stem-clasping upper leaves - red deadnettle has all stalked leaves, while white and spotted deadnettles are much larger perennial plants.

Yellow archangel stands out from its deadnettle relatives primarily by its golden flowers - red deadnettle has pink-purple blooms, henbit has smaller purple flowers, and white deadnettle has white flowers.
Among its deadnettle relatives, spotted deadnettle is the only one with distinctive silvery-white leaf markings - red deadnettle and henbit have plain green leaves.
Among the deadnettles, cutleaf deadnettle stands out for its dramatically dissected leaves - much more deeply cut than red deadnettle's heart-shaped leaves or henbit's rounded, scalloped ones.
White deadnettle stands out from its relatives by its pure white flowers and perennial growth habit.
